questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Identify modal auxiliary verbs in spoken sentences.
questions.prompt: Listen to the teacher’s three short sentences. After each sentence, say the modal auxiliary you heard. Do not read the teacher’s script.
questions.answer: can; should; might.
questions.explanation: The listener identifies the auxiliary heard, not the action word following it.

markingGuide.description: Identifies can.
Identifies should.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Use modal auxiliary verbs in spoken sentences.
questions.prompt: Work with a partner in a live role-play. You need to borrow a ruler. Ask politely using could or may, listen to your partner’s answer and respond appropriately. Then swap roles.
questions.answer: Could I borrow your ruler, please? — Yes, you may. — Thank you. If the partner cannot lend it: That is all right; I will ask someone else. Accept other fitting exchanges.
questions.explanation: Score the learner’s own request and response, including an appropriate reaction to what the partner actually says.

markingGuide.description: Uses a suitable modal in a polite request.
Makes the request understandable and relevant.
Responds appropriately to the partner’s actual reply.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Discuss age-appropriate issues using modal auxiliary verbs.
questions.prompt: In a small group, discuss this fictional issue: everyone wants the first turn with a shared classroom game. Suggest a fair plan using should or could, give a reason and respond respectfully to another pupil’s idea.
questions.answer: We could take turns using a list. We should let everyone have a turn because the game belongs to the class. I agree with your idea about a time limit. Accept another fair plan and relevant response.
questions.explanation: The task assesses modal use and participation in an age-appropriate national-value discussion about fairness, not a compulsory single policy.

markingGuide.description: Uses at least one suitable modal for a proposal.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Use modal auxiliary verbs in spoken sentences.
questions.prompt: Speak two sentences about tomorrow’s class activity: one announces a definite plan using will; the other describes a possible change using might. Explain the difference in meaning.
questions.answer: We will arrange the books tomorrow. We might move the reading mat if the room is crowded. Will presents the plan as intended; might presents the change as possible.
questions.explanation: Accept varied sensible plans. This samples meanings in the stated context, not a universal rule that will always guarantees an event.

markingGuide.description: Uses will appropriately for the stated plan.
Uses might appropriately for a possibility.
Explains the difference between intention/plan and possibility.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: State the meaning and basic patterns of question tags.
questions.prompt: Explain aloud what a question tag is. Give an original example with a positive statement and a negative tag, and say how the tag connects to the statement.
questions.answer: A question tag is a short question added to a statement. For example, The boxes are ready, aren’t they? The auxiliary matches are, the negative tag contrasts with the positive statement, and they refers to the boxes.
questions.explanation: The opposite-polarity pattern is a basic classroom pattern, not the only possible conversational tag construction.

markingGuide.description: Explains a short question added to a statement.
Gives a suitable original positive-statement/negative-tag example.
Explains a matching auxiliary and subject reference.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Oral Composition: Descriptive and Narrative Composition
questions.learningObjective: Narrate highlights of a village or market visit orally.
questions.prompt: Give an oral narration of a market visit. You may use an imagined visit. Describe arrival, one buying or selling event and how the visit ended. Tell events in a clear order and include one detail that helps the listener picture the market.
questions.answer: On Saturday I went to a small market with my aunt. We passed baskets of bright tomatoes before stopping at a yam stall. My aunt compared two yams and paid for one. We thanked the seller and returned home before noon. Accept a different coherent market visit.
questions.explanation: An imagined route samples oral narration; it does not establish that a pupil witnessed a real market event. No personal trip or expenditure is required.

markingGuide.description: Establishes a market setting and arrival.
Develops a relevant buying/selling event.
Orders events with a clear ending.
Uses intelligible connected speech and a helpful descriptive detail.

questions.learningObjective: Identify major features of an event: time, place, occasion and significance.
questions.prompt: Listen to a short report about a fictional event. Retell its time, place and occasion, then explain why the event mattered.

questions.topic: Aural Discrimination in Vowels and Consonants
questions.learningObjective: Discriminate between consonant sounds in heard words.
questions.prompt: Listen to four pairs of words. For each pair, say same or different according to the first consonant sound. The teacher will not show you the words.
questions.answer: Different; same; different; same.
questions.explanation: The comparison concerns initial consonant sounds, not spelling or whole-word meanings. Targets use /ʃ/ and /tʃ/.

markingGuide.description: Correctly classifies pairs 1 and 2.
Correctly classifies pairs 3 and 4.

questions.examinerScript: Precheck a clear /ʃ/–/tʃ/ contrast in the teaching model. Explain the same/different task with an unrelated practice pair. questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: State the meaning of stress in speech.
questions.prompt: Explain word stress aloud. Say the word table and show which part is more prominent without shouting.
questions.answer: Word stress makes one syllable more prominent than another. In table, the first syllable is prominent: TAble.
questions.explanation: Prominence can involve duration, pitch and clarity as well as loudness. It does not mean shouting every word.

markingGuide.description: Explains prominence of one syllable.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Discuss word stress and sentence stress.
questions.prompt: Demonstrate the difference between word stress and sentence stress. First say happy with its usual word stress. Then say I chose the BLUE folder to correct someone who thought you chose a red folder. Explain the two different choices of emphasis.
questions.answer: HAPpy has first-syllable word stress. Prominence on BLUE selects the colour being corrected within the sentence.
questions.explanation: Word stress concerns syllables within a word; sentence stress can highlight information or contrast. Capital letters are rehearsal cues rather than a request to shout.

markingGuide.description: Demonstrates HAPpy with first-syllable prominence.
Highlights blue naturally in the sentence.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Apply stress placement in selected common words without treating tendencies as universal rules.
questions.prompt: Say these four words aloud using the teacher-prechecked classroom patterns: table, happy, arrive, begin. Then group them orally according to whether the first or second syllable is stressed.
questions.answer: TAble and HAPpy have first-syllable stress; aRRIVE and beGIN have second-syllable stress.
questions.explanation: These selected examples illustrate tendencies. Not every two-syllable noun/adjective or verb follows a single rule; dictionary/model checking remains necessary.

markingGuide.description: Produces the first-syllable pattern for table and happy.

questions.prompt: In a live correction, a partner says that Amina lent you the notebook. The fictional fact is that Amina lent you the atlas. Correct your partner in one sentence, using emphasis to make the changed item clear.
questions.answer: Amina lent me the ATLAS, not the notebook. Accept a natural equivalent with clear focus on atlas.
questions.explanation: The task uses sentence prominence to signal the corrected information rather than changing the word’s ordinary internal stress.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: State the meaning of intonation.
questions.prompt: Explain intonation aloud. Demonstrate it by saying the same short phrase once with your pitch moving up at the end and once with it moving down.
questions.answer: Intonation is the movement of pitch across speech. The learner demonstrates a rise and a fall, for example with The door is open.
questions.explanation: Pitch movement is different from simply speaking louder or faster. This task identifies the feature before assigning a contextual meaning.

markingGuide.description: Explains pitch movement.
Demonstrates an audible rise and fall.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: State and demonstrate contextual uses of rising and falling intonation.
questions.prompt: Role-play these two situations aloud. First, you do not know whether a partner has finished and ask Have you finished? Second, you report that you have finished and say I have finished. Use a clear classroom rising pattern for the first and a falling pattern for the second, then explain the different purposes.
questions.answer: The learner uses a rise for the genuine yes/no information question and a fall for the completion report, explaining asking versus reporting.
questions.explanation: These are appropriate practice choices in the specified situations, not an absolute rule that every question rises or every statement falls.

markingGuide.description: Demonstrates the requested rise in the information question.
Demonstrates the requested fall in the report.
Explains asking for information versus reporting completion.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain how intonation can change meaning.
questions.prompt: Say The hall is ready, isn’t it? in two short role-plays: first you are unsure and want to find out; next you can see that it is ready and invite agreement. Explain how your final pitch helps show the difference.
questions.answer: A final rise on isn’t it? can signal the genuine uncertainty; a fall can invite agreement when the speaker expects confirmation.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary pattern stays the same while intonation and context affect the intended meaning. Accept a clear demonstration and explanation consistent with the taught model.

markingGuide.description: Uses a rise for the uncertainty role.
Uses a fall for inviting agreement.
Connects the pitch choices to the stated meanings.

questions.passage:
The Patient Builder
I set a little block in place,
Then watched my tower sway;
I made the base a little wide,
And tried another way.
One careful step, another step,
The work began to stand;
I learnt that trying once again
Could strengthen heart and hand.

questions.answer: The pupil sings the supplied original words with an audible tune and steady phrases. Accept any simple original tune that fits; musical sophistication and one exact melody are not required.

markingGuide.description: Sings with a discernible tune rather than only speaking.
Keeps the main words intelligible and in sequence.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Discuss a poem’s meaning, effect and theme orally.
questions.prompt: Discuss The Patient Builder aloud. Explain what happens after the tower sways, suggest its main theme and say how the repeated idea of another step affects the poem.
questions.answer: The speaker widens the base and tries again. A suitable theme is patient improvement through repeated effort. The repeated steps suggest steady progress rather than instant success. Accept supported alternative wording.
questions.explanation: This is an oral discussion of meaning, effect and theme, with evidence from the original text.

markingGuide.description: Explains the repair/change and further attempt.
States a supported theme about persistence or careful improvement.
Explains how the repeated steps reinforce steady effort.
